title.en: Shun Asks Yao How He Employs His Faculties (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 舜問堯天子之用心（莊子）

region.en: Yao's court at Fen-yang (Linfen, Shanxi, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Shun asks Yao how he employs his faculties. Yao describes his pity for the orphan and widow; Shun answers that this is good but not great — be passive like the virtue of God, whose sun and moon shine and seasons revolve without effort. Yao cries out that he has been making a muddle: You are in accord with God; I am in accord with man.
summary.zh: 舜問於堯：天王之用心何如？堯曰：吾不敖無告，不廢窮民，嘉孺子而哀婦人。舜曰：天德而出寧——日月照而四時行，若晝夜之有經，雲行而雨施矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Of old, Shun asked Yao, saying, "How does your Majesty employ your faculties?" "I am not arrogant towards the defenceless," replied Yao. "I do not neglect the poor. I grieve for those who die. I pity the orphan. I sympathise with the widow. Beyond this, nothing." "Good indeed!" cried Shun, "but yet not great." "How so?" inquired Yao. "Be passive," said Shun, "like the virtue of God. The sun and moon shine; the four seasons revolve; day and night alternate; clouds come and rain falls." "Alas!" cried Yao, "what a muddle I have been making. You are in accord with God; I am in accord with man."

title.en: Confucius Deposits His Works with Lao Tan (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子西藏書於周，往見老聃（莊子）

region.en: The Chou imperial library, Luoyang (Henan, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Going west to place his works in the Chou imperial library, Confucius is counselled to interview the retired librarian Lao Tan — who interrupts the exposition of his twelve canons with 'This is all nonsense.' Charity and duty to one's neighbour, Lao Tzŭ argues, are not part of man's original nature: universal love contradicts itself, the elimination of self is a manifestation of self; follow the Tao of the unceasing sun and moon.
summary.zh: 孔子西藏書於周室，往見老聃。老聃曰：亦取其大要而已——子所言者，其人與骨皆已朽矣。仁義，先王之蘧廬也；無私，乃私也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Confucius-and-Laozi interview topos, paralleled in Shiji 63 and the Laojun hagiography. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Confucius was going west to place his works in the Imperial library of the House of Chou, Tzŭ Lu counselled him, saying, "I have heard that a certain librarian of the Chêng department, by name Lao Tan, has resigned and retired into private life. Now as you, Sir, wish to deposit your works, it would be advisable to go and interview him." "Certainly," said Confucius; and he thereupon went to see Lao Tzŭ. The latter would not hear of the proposal; so Confucius began to expound the doctrines of his twelve canons, in order to convince Lao Tzŭ. "This is all nonsense," cried Lao Tzŭ, interrupting him. "Tell me what are your criteria." "Charity," replied Confucius, "and duty towards one's neighbour."

"Tell me," said Lao Tzŭ, "in what consist charity and duty to one's neighbour?" "They consist," answered Confucius, "in a capacity for rejoicing in all things; in universal love, without the element of self. These are the characteristics of charity and duty to one's neighbour." "What stuff!" cried Lao Tzŭ. "Does not universal love contradict itself? Is not your elimination of self a positive manifestation of self? Sir, if you would cause the empire not to lose its source of nourishment,--there is the universe, its regularity is unceasing; there are the sun and moon, their brightness is unceasing; there are the stars, their groupings never change; there are birds and beasts, they flock together without varying; there are trees and shrubs, they grow upwards without exception, Be like these; follow TAO; and you will be perfect. Why then these vain struggles after charity and duty to one's neighbour, as though beating a drum in search of a fugitive. Alas! Sir, you have brought much confusion into the mind of man."

title.en: The Wheelwright and the Dregs of the Ancients (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The hall of Duke Huan of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊桓公之堂（今山東臨淄）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Duke Huan reads in his hall while a wheelwright works below; flinging down his hammer, the wheelwright tells the Duke that the words of the dead Sages are only the dregs of the ancients. Wheel-making is a mysterious art of co-ordination between mind and hand that he cannot teach even his own son — and what the ancients could not impart died with them.
summary.zh: 桓公讀書於堂上，輪扁斲輪於堂下，釋椎鑿而上：君之所讀者，古人之糟魄已夫。斲輪徐則甘而不固，疾則苦而不入；得之於手而應於心，口不能言，臣不能以喻臣之子。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Huan was one day reading in his hall, when a wheelwright who was working below, flung down his hammer and chisel, and mounting the steps said, "What words may your Highness be studying?" "I am studying the words of the Sages," replied the Duke. "Are the Sages alive?" asked the wheelwright. "No," answered the Duke; "they are dead." "Then the words your Highness is studying," rejoined the wheelwright, "are only the dregs of the ancients."

"Let me take an illustration," said the wheelwright, "from my own trade. In making a wheel, if you work too slowly, you can't make it firm; if you work too fast, the spokes won't fit in. You must go neither too slowly nor too fast. There must be co-ordination of mind and hand. Words cannot explain what it is, but there is some mysterious art herein. I cannot teach it to my son; nor can he learn it from me. Consequently, though seventy years of age, I am still making wheels in my old age. If the ancients, together with what they could not impart, are dead and gone, then what your Highness is studying must be the dregs."

title.en: Had You Called Me a Horse, I Should Have Considered Myself a Horse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 呼我牛也而謂之牛（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Shih Ch'êng Ch'i walks many stages to insult the Sage Lao Tzŭ for turning his sister out of doors while rats feast on his leavings. The Sage keeps silent; the next day he answers that he makes no pretension: had you called me an ox, I should have considered myself an ox — if men class you in accordance with truth and you reject the classification, you only double the reproach.
summary.zh: 士成綺見老子而問曰：吾聞夫子聖人也……觀於其室，不見其有所謂仁義也。老子曰：吾服也恆服，吾非以服有怍——呼我牛也而謂之牛，呼我馬也而謂之馬。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Shih Ch'êng Ch'i visited Lao Tzŭ, and addressed him, saying, "Having heard, Sir, that you were a Sage, I put aside all thought of distance to come and visit you. Travelling many stages, the soles of my feet thickened, but I did not venture to rest. And now I see you are not a Sage. While rats feasted off your leavings, you turned your sister out of doors. This is not charity. Though you have no lack of food, raw and cooked, you are stingy beyond all bounds."

At this Lao Tzŭ was silent and made no reply; and the next day Shih Ch'êng Ch'i came again and said, "Before, I was rude to you; now, I am sorry. How is this?" "I have no pretension," replied Lao Tzŭ, "to be possessed of cunning knowledge nor of divine wisdom. Had you yesterday called me an ox, I should have considered myself an ox. Had you called me a horse, I should have considered myself a horse. For if men class you in accordance with truth, and you reject the classification, you only double the reproach. My humility is natural humility. It is not humility for humility's sake."
